title: connectors-ci: huge slowdown in gradle task run following Dagger engine upgrade to > 0.5.3
body: I observe a large slowdown when running tests for our Java connectors after upgrading Dagger. For destination-s3, a nightly run using the earlier setup built the connector tar in 2m56s and ran integration tests in 8m54s. After the upgrade to Dagger 0.6.2, building the tar took 10m20s and integration tests took 17m10s. I can run the tar build locally without the Dagger cache in about six minutes. The first run on 0.6.2 also took about ten minutes to build the tar, so I suspect the Dagger upgrade introduced the regression.

symptoms_visible: After upgrading to Dagger 0.6.2, destination-s3's connector tar build takes about 10 minutes instead of under 3 minutes, and its integration tests take about 17 minutes instead of under 9 minutes.
N0.label: N0 connector test slowdown reported

symptoms_visible: After reverting the runners and SDK to 0.5.4, the connector test runs at its original speed again.
N1.label: N1 temporary rollback restores performance

symptoms_visible: The reverted 0.5.4 setup remains fast, while the 0.6.2 setup is the one showing the large connector-test slowdown.
N2.label: N2 fast setup pins identified

symptoms_visible: The reverted run completes the distTar step in 439.24 seconds even though it appears to use 16 CPUs.
N3.label: N3 CPU comparison reported

symptoms_visible: After setting the runner-host environment variable back, the connector pipeline runs at its expected speed again.
N_terminal.label: terminal performance restored

solution.intent: Temporarily revert the Dagger runners and SDK to the previously fast 0.5.4 configuration while investigating the upgrade-related difference.
solution.concrete_example: Revert the runners and SDK to 0.5.4 and rerun destination-s3 to determine whether the earlier performance returns.

edges.comment: Opening follow-up c0, reporter's Airbyte system: the reporter reverted runners and SDK to 0.5.4 and observed the original speed return. This is a successful temporary mitigation and comparison point, not the final root-cause fix.

question_patterns: What exact Engine and CLI configuration was used by the fast reverted run?
Can you share the pinned Engine image and CLI revision from the setup that restored the original speed?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the 0.5.4 SDK, we also pinned the Engine to registry.dagger.io/engine:main@sha256:935a9df9d9480f1f6a3f41c4caa65ad4304c99e4371610f45748b16ab46cfc7c and the CLI to 6ed6264f1c4efbf84d310a104b57ef1bc57d57b0.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The fast and slow runs used the same SDK, Engine image, CLI revision, and workflow configuration.
The fast setup used the same Engine digest but a nearby 0.5.x SDK patch release.

edges.comment: Thread c3, reporter's Airbyte configuration: the reporter supplied the exact Engine digest and CLI commit used with the fast 0.5.4 SDK setup.

question_patterns: How many CPUs did the fast reverted run appear to use, and how long did its distTar step take?
Can you compare the runner capacity and Gradle duration for the reverted run?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I think the reverted run uses 16 CPUs, and its distTar step took 439.24 seconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The fast run used 32 CPUs, while every slow run used only 16 CPUs.
The fast run still appears to use 16 CPUs, with the distTar step varying by a few seconds.

edges.comment: Thread c6-c7: Gerhard raised differing CPU counts as a possible environmental factor; the reporter then identified a fast reverted run that appeared to use 16 CPUs and reported its raw 439.24-second distTar duration. The answer does not claim what caused the slowdown.

solution.intent: Restore the environment variable that directs Dagger to Airbyte's already provisioned Engine, preferably configuring it on the self-hosted runner, then rerun the connector pipeline to verify that performance is restored.
solution.concrete_example: Set _EXPERIMENTAL_DAGGER_RUNNER_HOST again so the workflow uses the provisioned Airbyte Engine rather than an auto-provisioned Docker Engine. Keep the infra-specific value on the self-hosted runner where possible, then rerun destination-s3 and compare its distTar and integration-test durations.
solution.inference_hint: The Dagger engineers compared the workflow diff and Engine identities. They inferred that removing _EXPERIMENTAL_DAGGER_RUNNER_HOST caused the 0.6.2 workflow to use an auto-provisioned Docker Engine, identified by a random container-like name, rather than Airbyte's provisioned Engine. That diagnosis is engineer-side interpretation; the reporter supplied timings, configuration details, and the successful post-change rerun.

edges.comment: Thread c12-c18, reporter's Airbyte pipeline: Dagger maintainers connected the random Engine identity to auto-provisioning and found that the upgrade diff removed _EXPERIMENTAL_DAGGER_RUNNER_HOST. The reporter restored it in c16-c17 and confirmed that this solved the performance issue. Gerhard then recommended placing the variable on the self-hosted runner because that is where the Engine integration is configured. The later Dagger release-version coordination is intentionally excluded from scoring.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the upgrade removed _EXPERIMENTAL_DAGGER_RUNNER_HOST, causing Dagger to auto-provision a different Docker Engine instead of using Airbyte's existing provisioned Engine; the slowdown was not an intrinsic Gradle regression in Dagger 0.6.2.

Must ground the diagnosis in the observed comparison: the 0.6.2 path was slow, reverting the Dagger setup restored speed, and a fast reverted run completed distTar in 439.24 seconds despite appearing to use 16 CPUs.
Must restore the runner-host environment variable so the pipeline uses the provisioned Engine; configuring this infra-specific value on the self-hosted runner is the preferred durable placement.
Must not treat permanent rollback to Dagger 0.5.4 as the final fix; it was a temporary mitigation that helped isolate the configuration difference.
Must ask the reporter to rerun the connector pipeline and compare its timings, and must only declare resolution after the reporter confirms that restoring the variable fixed performance.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Airbyte connector-infrastructure engineer who can modify CI runner, Dagger Engine, CLI, and SDK configuration; can compare Gradle scans, Dagger Cloud runs, CPU allocation, and pinned image digests.
persona_hint.communication_style: Technical, concise, and collaborative; supplies exact run links, durations, image digests, and commit hashes; openly labels uncertain observations such as CPU count and quickly tests maintainers' configuration suggestions.
